explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. John says, "…He loved them to the very end." Not halfway, and not until it got hard. Whatever comes next that night, His love is already there.

The Passover Feast tells us when this happens. It's just before the Feast, but it isn't where His love stops. John says Jesus "loved them to the very end." That's a finish line much farther down the road than a holiday.
Friend, go look for the fine print in that verse. There isn't any. John says, "He loved them to the very end." It has no "as long as" and no conditions.

Yes, baker. John says "the devil had already put into the heart of Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot, to betray Jesus." That's heavy, so I'll say it plainly and leave it there. Notice the words "already." This was underway before the meal even got going.

Pontius Pilate was the governor (Matthew 27:2), and he does show up in Jesus' story later. But John 13:2 doesn't name him here. The text says it was the devil who put this into Judas' heart. Pilate hasn't even walked into this room yet.

King Herod was ruling when Jesus was born (Matthew 2:1), so he's a real name in Jesus' story. But he isn't the one in this verse. John says the devil put it into Judas' heart to betray Jesus. Herod isn't at this supper at all.

That's right. John says Jesus knew "that He had come from God and was returning to God." So He knows where He started and where He's headed. Keep that in mind, because it makes what He does next even bigger.
It's true, friend. John says Jesus knew that "He had come from God and was returning to God." So He knows where He came from and where He's going. Both ends of the road are clear to Him.

A basin, baker. John says Jesus "poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples' feet." It's a plain, everyday tub for a plain, everyday job. And the One doing the job is anything but plain.
Close, friend, but John doesn't say jar. He says Jesus "poured water into a basin." A basin is wide and open, which is the kind of thing you'd want for washing feet. I'd want one for flour spills.
A cup would be a very long evening for twelve pairs of feet. John says Jesus "poured water into a basin." That's the vessel in this verse.

That's it. Jesus tells Peter, "You do not realize now what I am doing, but later you will understand." So Peter doesn't get it yet, and Jesus says that's okay for now. Plenty of my batches made sense only after they came out of the oven.
It's true, baker. Jesus tells Peter, "You do not realize now what I am doing, but later you will understand." He doesn't leave Peter hanging. He promises that understanding is coming.

explanations.answer: He says Jesus will never wash his feet
explanations.explanation: Yep. Peter tells Him, "Never shall You wash my feet!" Jesus just said understanding would come later, and Peter answers right now with a flat no. I bet my mustache would've done the same twitch.

explanations.answer: He asks to wash Jesus' feet first
explanations.explanation: That's a kind idea, baker, but it isn't what Peter says. John records, "Never shall You wash my feet!" Peter pushes back. He doesn't offer a trade.

explanations.answer: He says he will wait until later
explanations.explanation: Jesus is the one who mentions later: "later you will understand." Peter doesn't take the offer. He answers, "Never shall You wash my feet!" Not later. Never.

explanations.answer: His hands and head washed too
explanations.explanation: Right. Peter says, "Then, Lord, not only my feet, but my hands and my head as well!" He heard "no part with Me" and changed course fast. Whatever else you say about Peter, he doesn't do things halfway.
Not quite, friend. Peter doesn't trade feet for hands. He says, "not only my feet, but my hands and my head as well!" He wants more washed, not less.

John doesn't have Peter bargaining about timing. After hearing "you have no part with Me," he says, "Then, Lord, not only my feet, but my hands and my head as well!" That's a bigger ask, not a later one.

Almost, but Jesus says something different. After the part about being completely clean, He tells Peter, "And you are clean, though not all of you." So He doesn't say every one of them is clean. That little "though" matters.
That's right, baker. Jesus says, "And you are clean, though not all of you." He doesn't call every disciple clean. John explains why in the very next verse.

explanations.answer: He knew who would betray Him
explanations.explanation: Yes. John says, "For He knew who would betray Him. That is why He said, 'Not all of you are clean.'" Jesus isn't guessing here, because He knows. And He washed those feet anyway.

That's a reasonable guess, but John never says it. He tells us the reason: "For He knew who would betray Him." The text ties "not all of you are clean" to the betrayal, not to anybody's bath schedule.
John doesn't mention anyone running late, friend. He says, "For He knew who would betray Him. That is why He said, 'Not all of you are clean.'" The reason is the betrayal.
Yes, baker. Jesus says, "You call Me Teacher and Lord, and rightly so, because I am." He doesn't wave the titles away. He says they fit.
It's true, friend. Jesus says, "You call Me Teacher and Lord, and rightly so, because I am." He agrees with the titles. And then He shows what a Teacher and Lord does with a towel.
That's it. Jesus says, "So if I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also should wash one another's feet." He doesn't stop at telling them what He did. He points them toward each other.
Good thought, baker, but listen to the wording. Jesus says they should wash "one another's feet." That means they wash each other's. He isn't asking for the favor back.

explanations.answer: Never let Him do it again
explanations.explanation: That sounds like Peter earlier, friend. But Jesus says something else: "you also should wash one another's feet." He's not telling them to refuse. He's telling them to do likewise.

Yes. Jesus says, "no servant is greater than his master, nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him." Those two pairs sit side by side. And He opens it with "Truly, truly," so it's worth underlining.
A king is a good guess, baker, but that's not the word in this verse. Jesus says, "nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him." The pairing is servant and master, then messenger and sender.
I like the family feel, but that isn't what Jesus says. The verse reads, "nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him." Messenger and sender. A brother never shows up in that line.
Careful, friend. Jesus says, "If you know these things, you will be blessed if you do them." The blessing is tied to doing, not only knowing. Knowing is where it starts.
That's right, baker. Jesus says, "If you know these things, you will be blessed if you do them." Knowing alone isn't the promise. It's the doing that comes with the blessing.

Right. Jesus quotes the Scripture: "The one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me." (Psalm 41:9) So it's someone who sits at His table and shares His bread. That's close, and it's why this hurts to read.

explanations.answer: A servant of the high priest
explanations.explanation: No servant of the high priest appears in this verse, baker. Jesus quotes, "The one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me." (Psalm 41:9) It's someone close enough to share His bread.
There's no soldier in the quote, friend. Jesus says, "The one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me." (Psalm 41:9) The person described is at the table with Him.

That's it. Jesus says, "I am telling you now before it happens, so that when it comes to pass, you will believe that I am He." He tells them first so that when it happens, they'll believe. He's thinking ahead for them.

explanations.answer: So that they can stop it
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't say that, baker. He says He's telling them now "so that when it comes to pass, you will believe that I am He." The goal is belief, not a rescue plan.

explanations.answer: So that they will tell others
explanations.explanation: Telling others is a good thing, friend, but it isn't the reason given here. Jesus says, "I am telling you now before it happens, so that when it comes to pass, you will believe that I am He." The reason is belief.
Yes, baker. Jesus says, "whoever receives Me receives the One who sent Me." Receiving Jesus is tied right to the One who sent Him. And it follows the line of the one He sends, too.
The prophets are important, friend, but Jesus doesn't name them here. He says, "whoever receives Me receives the One who sent Me." The link He draws goes to the One who sent Him.
Angels don't appear in this verse, baker. Jesus says, "whoever receives Me receives the One who sent Me." That's the connection He gives.
